articles.title: Catch a leftover noindex before it ships: a small check for CI
articles.excerpt: Add a smoke test to your deploy that fetches your key URLs and fails if any of them says "do not index". It takes about 40 lines, and it catches the most expensive small mistake in a site launch: a no…
articles.body: Add a smoke test to your deploy that fetches your key URLs and fails if any of them says "do not index". It takes about 40 lines, and it catches the most expensive small mistake in a site launch: a noindex that was right on staging and stayed on in production. The mistake is common after a redesign. The staging site is blocked on purpose. Someone copies a config, a layout or a header rule across, and nobody looks at it again. Pages drop out of search over the next weeks, and the cause is invisible in the browser because the page looks fine. Where "do not index" can hide There are four places. A good check reads all four. The meta tag in the HTML head: <meta name="robots" content="noindex"> . It can also be addressed to one bot, such as googlebot . The X-Robots-Tag response header.

articles.body: Deciding whether it is okay to use ai to write website content comes down to how well the final material serves human readers rather than the tools used to produce it. Google evaluates pages based on quality and originality instead of the generation method. Automated text is permitted if it prioritizes people over search-ranking manipulation, though human oversight remains essential to protect credibility and avoid algorithmic penalties. Search engines focus entirely on whether a page solves the user problem that prompted the search query. What search engines say about automated text Google evaluates website content based on how well it serves human readers rather than the tools used to produce it.

articles.body: Filipino small businesses live on social media. Your favorite milk tea shop? It probably runs on Facebook Page messages and TikTok videos. Not a website. So when those shops start buying boosts for their posts, things get chaotic fast. Screenshots in Messenger. Orders tracked in a notebook. Payments scattered across GCash receipts. This post shows a simple Node.js setup that fixes that. We'll send orders to an SMM panel API, store them and show a clean status board. Nothing fancy. Just practical. Why a tracker even matters Here's the thing. A shop owner doesn't care about API responses. She cares about three questions: Did my order start? How much is done? Did I get refunded for anything that failed? Answer those clearly and you've built something people will actually use.

articles.title: Two screens, two aspect ratios: what changes when you cut a wallpaper twice
articles.excerpt: Most wallpaper advice assumes one display. The iPhone Duo has two, and they are not the same shape. Apple lists the inner panel at 1878 x 2670 and the cover at 1398 x 2034. Written the way you actuall…
articles.body: Most wallpaper advice assumes one display. The iPhone Duo has two, and they are not the same shape. Apple lists the inner panel at 1878 x 2670 and the cover at 1398 x 2034. Written the way you actually hold the phone open, that gives three rectangles: Surface Pixels Ratio (w/h) Inner, open and sideways 2670 x 1878 1.4217 Inner, open and upright 1878 x 2670 0.7034 Cover, closed 1398 x 2034 0.6873 The last two matter. The cover is 2.3% narrower than the inner screen. That is small enough to miss in a mockup and large enough to notice on a photograph: a subject that sits comfortably on the inside creeps toward the edge once the phone is closed. There is a second problem the ratio table does not show. The hinge runs through the middle of the inner display.

articles.title: package.json is the file everyone edits and nobody lints — the footguns that only fail in CI
articles.excerpt: package.json is the most-edited JSON file in the JavaScript ecosystem. It's also the one npm validates least. npm install will happily accept a file that breaks publishing, breaks your teammates' npm…
articles.body: package.json is the most-edited JSON file in the JavaScript ecosystem. It's also the one npm validates least. npm install will happily accept a file that breaks publishing, breaks your teammates' npm ci , or breaks your license compliance review — and tell you nothing until the worst possible moment. I got burned by this enough times that I wrote a linter for it. Here's what I check for, and a ~20-line version you can steal right now. What npm doesn't catch 1. type typos. "type": "module" vs "type": "moduel" . npm ignores unknown values silently; your ESM files suddenly run as CommonJS and the error surfaces three dependencies deep. 2. Non-string scripts. "scripts": { "build": ["webpack"] } — an array instead of a string.

articles.title: Reframing landscape video to 9:16 in the browser with WebCodecs (no upload)
articles.excerpt: Most "make my video vertical" tools work the same way: upload your file, wait, download the result. For a 2 GB podcast recording that means waiting on the upload before you can even start, and it mean…
articles.body: Most "make my video vertical" tools work the same way: upload your file, wait, download the result. For a 2 GB podcast recording that means waiting on the upload before you can even start, and it means your footage now lives on someone else's server. Browsers can do this locally now. WebCodecs gives JavaScript access to the device's hardware video decoder and encoder, so I built Vertical Video Maker , a 16:9 → 9:16 (or 4:5 / 1:1) converter where the file never leaves the device. Here's how it works and what bit me along the way. The pipeline File ─► demux (MP4/MOV/WebM) ─► decode ─► draw each frame on a canvas ─► encode H.264 ─► mux MP4 ─► Blob WebCodecs only does the codec part ( VideoDecoder / VideoEncoder ). It doesn't read or write containers, so you need something to demux and mux.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 21, 1676: Danish astronomer discovers speed of light — by accident — while observing Jupiter's moon Io
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of lightwhile observing Jupiter and its moon volcanic moon Io. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light . Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast. Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io . He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years. To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule.

articles.excerpt: Assimilate this! How cyber-zombies and the "birth of 'Star Trek'" gave Jean-Luc Picard one of his finest hours.
articles.body: Following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing , there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard . "The Inner Light"'s life in 25 minutes is a strong contender, as are the courtroom grandstanding in "The Measure of a Man" and his insistence (under extreme torture) that "there are four lights!" in "Chain of Command". But for this writer's money, it's hard to look past a nine-minute sequence in "Star Trek: First Contact", which turns 30 this weekend.

articles.title: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
articles.excerpt: Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life. The AI lab behind Claude went public…
articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life. The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet. The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years.

articles.title: SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper stage ever caught by 'chopsticks,' Elon Musk says
articles.excerpt: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. Rather, it will go on display as a museum piece, according to company founder and CEO Elon Musk.
articles.body: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship 's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX 's Starbase site in South Texas. Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk , who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen. "In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit .

articles.title: European-Japanese BepiColombo probe arrives in orbit around Mercury today
articles.excerpt: The BepiColombo spacecraft will finally arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet.
articles.body: Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth. The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency ( JAXA ) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet. The big moment will come after an orbit-insertion burn, which is scheduled to begin today at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT) and last for 37 minutes. BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio.
